newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish parliament debates anti-biker legislation.
newsitem.headline: Danish parliament debates anti-biker legislation.

text.p: Denmark's parliament launched on Thursday into what promised to be a marathon final debate on legislation to curb biker gang warfare raging in a country normally noted for law-abiding tranquillity.

"The house has started with the second reading of the bill. If all goes well, and none of it has to be returned to committee for further treatment, we are 99.9 percent sure the legislation will be passed at its third and last reading later today," a parliamentary secretariat official told Reuters.
"The session could be something of a marathon," she added.
The government's emergency biker legislation bill is assured broad parliamentary support.

Aimed at shutting down attack-prone gang buildings in residential neighbourhoods, it is likely to become law next week, ministry officials said, rather than by the weekend as Danish Justice Minister Bjoern Westh had originally pledged.
Amendments sought by parliamentarians after a committee hearing on Monday were inserted in the bill prior to its second and third readings on Thursday.
After passage, three working days must pass before Queen Margrethe can sign it into law.

The final parliamentary processing of the biker bill comes on the eve of a meeting of justice ministers from Finland, Norway and Sweden to be hosted in Copenhagen by Danish Justice Minister Bjoern Westh on Friday and aimed at seeking a joint Nordic response to the bloody regional biker war.
Westh proposed the meeting after last Sunday's missile attack on the central Copenhagen headquarters of the Hell's Angels motorcycle gang, in which two people were killed.
Attending the Nordic council-of-war, hosted by Westh, will be Swedish Justice Minister Laila Freivalds and her Norwegian and Finnish counterparts, Grete Faremo and Kari Hakamies.
Danish Justice Ministry spokesman Henning Bach Christensen told Reuters that the meeting had been called at such short notice that an agenda was still being drafted.
"But I think (the ministers) will try and carry away something solid," he said.
Police regard the Bandido gang, which has been battling the dominant Hell's Angels for the past three years, as the main suspect in last Sunday's missile attack in Copenhagen.
Six of the 17 injured in the blast were still in hospital on Thursday, all of them out of danger, and police were hunting for three main suspects, the national news agency Ritzau reported.

The shoulder-fired anti-tank rocket used in the attack was one of a batch stolen from army stores in neighbouring Sweden in 1994. Other missiles from the break-in were fired at two Hell's Angels' clubhouses in different areas of Denmark last April.
The association of Danish local authorities says there are now about 40 biker strongholds spread across the country.

Sweden and Norway have both said that they will study details of the new Danish law -- the first in a promised package to give police wider gang-busting powers -- to see if it might be suitable for them.
Conflict between the gangs, both local offshoots of U.S. groups with extensive European networks, began almost as soon as the Bandidos set up shop in the region in the summer of 1993.

In February 1994 a member of the Hell's Angels-affiliated Rednecks died in a gunfight after walking -- reportedly by accident -- into a Bandidos meeting at a night club in the Swedish port of Helsingborg.

The then newly-elected president of the Bandidos, Mikael Ljunggren, was killed by a sniper as he rode his motorcycle north of the city in July 1995, in an ambush that investigators said could have been either a Hell's Angels attack or the work of fellow gang members opposed to his leadership.
In March this year, attackers shot dead a Bandidos leader in the Finnish capital, Helsinki, and a Danish Bandido died in an ambush outside Copenhagen airport 10 days later.
A Danish Bandidos member was fatally shot in the head near the Norwegian town of Drammen in July.
